papers.title: Local translation of endosome-associated lc3b mRNA in axons contributes to endosomal clearance.
papers.summary: This paper shows that LC3B mRNA, a key autophagy-related transcript, is transported into axons and locally translated right at endosomes. This local production of LC3B protein helps convert endosomes into autophagic structures, promoting their clearance. The findings suggest that axons rely on localized translation, rather than only importing preformed protein from the cell body, to maintain endosomal and autophagic homeostasis far from the soma.
papers.why: This directly supports the project's focus on mitophagy and autophagy in neurons by revealing a local, axon-specific translational mechanism controlling autophagosome formation and endosomal clearance, relevant to understanding neuronal proteostasis that could be mapped spatially alongside metabolomic and transcriptomic profiles.
papers.figure: A figure showing colocalization of lc3b mRNA, ribosomes, and endosomal markers along axons, ideally with quantification of local translation events.

papers.title: Catalpol Protects Against MPP<sup>+</sup>-Induced Neurotoxicity by Targeting PINK1/DJ-1-Mediated Mitophagy and the TrkB/Akt/BDNF/Bcl-2 Axis.
papers.summary: This study examines whether catalpol, a plant-derived compound, can protect neurons from damage caused by MPP+, a toxin used to model Parkinson's disease. The researchers focused on how catalpol influences mitophagy, the process cells use to clear damaged mitochondria, specifically through the PINK1/DJ-1 pathway. They also looked at a survival signaling pathway involving TrkB, Akt, BDNF, and Bcl-2, finding that catalpol activates these protective mechanisms to reduce neurotoxicity.
papers.why: This paper offers direct mechanistic insight into PINK1-mediated mitophagy in neurons, a core pathway relevant to the mitophagy/autophagy focus of the PhD project, even though it centers on a pharmacological intervention rather than spatial omics or interneuron biology.
papers.figure: A figure showing mitophagy markers (e.g., PINK1, DJ-1, LC3-II/Parkin colocalization) alongside mitochondrial morphology in MPP+-treated neurons with and without catalpol treatment.

papers.title: Schizophrenia and bipolar disorder risk gene AKAP11 sustains cognitive function by regulating TFEB-mediated autophagy.
papers.summary: This paper investigates AKAP11, a gene linked to both schizophrenia and bipolar disorder risk, and shows it plays a role in regulating autophagy through the transcription factor TFEB. The researchers found that AKAP11 is important for maintaining normal cognitive function, likely by controlling how brain cells clear out damaged components via autophagy. When AKAP11 function is disrupted, autophagy regulation goes awry, which may help explain cognitive symptoms seen in these psychiatric disorders.
papers.why: This work connects a major psychiatric risk gene to TFEB-mediated autophagy in the brain, directly relevant to the project's focus on autophagy and mitophagy mechanisms in neurons and their impact on cognitive circuits.

papers.title: Repressor Element 1 Silencing Transcription Factor as a central regulator of autophagy and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease.
papers.summary: This paper discusses REST (Repressor Element 1 Silencing Transcription Factor) as a key regulator that links autophagy and neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease. REST is known to decline with aging and neurodegeneration, and its loss is thought to disrupt cellular clearance mechanisms while promoting inflammatory responses in the brain. The abstract itself provides no methodological or experimental details, only the topic focus.
papers.why: REST's role in coordinating autophagy and neuroinflammatory pathways in neurons could inform mechanistic hypotheses about mitophagy dysfunction in interneurons within your Alzheimer's-related spatial transcriptomics work.

papers.title: Kir6.2-KATP channel: A new target for manganese neurotoxicity induced autophagy impairment and oxidative stress injury.
papers.summary: This study investigates how manganese exposure causes neurotoxicity by disrupting the Kir6.2-KATP ion channel in neurons. The researchers found that manganese-induced dysfunction of this channel leads to impaired autophagy (the cell's waste-clearing process) and increased oxidative stress damage. Kir6.2-KATP is proposed as a novel molecular target that could explain how manganese harms brain cells and potentially be targeted therapeutically.
papers.why: This paper connects directly to the mitophagy/autophagy impairment focus of the profile by identifying a specific ion channel mechanism linking heavy metal neurotoxicity to autophagic dysfunction and oxidative stress in neurons.

papers.title: PIP4K2A Attenuates Cerebral Ischemia/Reperfusion Injury by Reducing the TRIB3-p62 Complex Burden and Modulating AKT/mTOR Signaling.
papers.summary: This study investigates how PIP4K2A, a lipid kinase, protects brain cells after ischemia/reperfusion injury (like a stroke). It works by reducing the buildup of a protein complex made of TRIB3 and p62, which is linked to autophagy regulation. The protective effect also involves changes in AKT/mTOR signaling, a key pathway controlling cell survival and autophagy.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it explores autophagy and p62-related pathways in neuronal stress response, directly connecting to mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms and AKT/mTOR signaling relevant to neuronal survival in the brain.

papers.title: Targeting Sirtuin Signaling in Parkinson's Disease and Neurodegeneration: Molecular Insights and Translational Potential.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how sirtuin proteins, a family of NAD+-dependent deacetylases, influence cellular pathways implicated in Parkinson's disease and other neurodegenerative conditions. It discusses molecular mechanisms by which sirtuins regulate mitochondrial function, oxidative stress responses, and protein aggregation in neurons. The review also explores translational strategies, including pharmacological activators of sirtuins, as potential therapeutic approaches for slowing neurodegeneration.
papers.why: Since sirtuins regulate mitochondrial quality control and autophagy pathways relevant to mitophagy in neurons, this review could inform mechanistic context for the project's focus on neuronal mitophagy in neurodegeneration.

papers.title: Targeting TOMM40 unleashes immunogenic mitophagy to facilitate antigen presentation and immunotherapy sensitization.
papers.summary: This paper investigates TOMM40, a protein on the outer mitochondrial membrane, as a target to trigger mitophagy (the selective clearance of mitochondria) in cancer cells. By blocking TOMM40, the researchers show that damaged mitochondria are processed in a way that boosts antigen presentation, making tumors more visible to the immune system. This 'immunogenic mitophagy' enhances the effectiveness of immunotherapy in the studied cancer models.
papers.why: Although this is a cancer immunotherapy study, its detailed mechanistic insights into TOMM40-mediated mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control could inform understanding of analogous mitophagy pathways relevant to neuronal health and neurodegeneration in the PhD project.
